prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "TJX COMPANIES INC /DE/" (ticker TJX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TJX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The TJX Companies, Inc.
result.industry: Off-price apparel and home fashions retail
markets: Off-price apparel and accessories (T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, Winners, TK Maxx)
Off-price home fashions and furnishings (HomeGoods, Homesense)
International off-price retail in Canada, Europe and Australia
E-commerce off-price (tjmaxx.com, marshalls.com, sierra.com, tkmaxx sites)

mission.statement: Our mission is to deliver great value to our customers every day.
mission.source: TJX Form 10-K for fiscal 2026 (Item 1, Business Overview)
mission.plain: Always sell good brand-name stuff for a lot less than other stores charge.

about.plain: TJX runs discount stores like T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods. Its buyers scoop up brand-name clothes, shoes and home items that other stores or makers have too much of, and buy them cheaply. Then it sells them in its stores for much less than department stores would charge. The racks change all the time, so shoppers come back often to hunt for bargains.
about.customers: Everyday shoppers, mostly middle-income families, who want brand-name clothes and home goods at bargain prices.
about.everyday: If you have ever hunted through the racks at T.J. Maxx or picked up a candle or throw pillow at HomeGoods, you have shopped at TJX.

money.part: Marmaxx (T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, Sierra in the US)
money.plain: discount brand-name clothes, shoes, accessories and home items
discount home decor, furniture and kitchen items

money.part: TJX International (TK Maxx and Homesense in Europe and Australia)
money.plain: the same bargain-store idea in the UK, Ireland, Germany, Poland, Austria, the Netherlands and Australia
discount clothes and home goods in Canada

money.part: New countries (Spain store opening from March 2026; Mexico and Middle East joint ventures)
money.plain: taking the off-price stores to new countries

result.summary: Yes: TJX is the world's largest off-price apparel and home retailer, with $60.4 billion of FY2026 sales, more than 1,400 buyers and about 21,000 vendors, so it can buy brand-name excess inventory at a scale no rival matches. That buying network and its treasure-hunt, fast-changing assortment are hard to copy and have produced steady comp growth (+5% in FY2026) and rising margins. The advantage rests on scale and know-how rather than technology or switching costs, so it stays tied to value-seeking shoppers and vendor relationships.

pricingPower.evidence: As a value retailer TJX does not lead on price rises; it promises prices well below full-price retailers. Still, during the 2025-26 tariff period it kept comp sales growing (+5% in FY2026, +6% in Q1 FY27, +4% in Q2 FY27) while gross margin rose from 30.6% in FY2025 to 31.0% in FY2026, showing it can manage price points and markdowns without losing traffic.

moats.evidence: T.J. Maxx, Marshalls, HomeGoods, Winners and TK Maxx are household names tied to 'brand names for less'; the stores sell other companies' brands, so the moat is the banner's value reputation rather than product brands.
Shoppers can walk into Ross, Burlington or Amazon at no cost; there is no membership or lock-in.

A mild two-sided effect: about 21,000 vendors sell to TJX because its 5,285 stores can absorb large volumes quickly, and that buying access attracts more shoppers, but it is not a classic network effect.

With $60.4 billion of FY2026 sales, more than twice Ross ($22.8 billion) and over five times Burlington ($11.6 billion), TJX buys in bigger volumes from more than 100 countries and runs distribution centres in six countries, giving it cheaper buying and spreading overhead.
The supply of branded excess inventory is finite and favours a few large buyers, but the US off-price market still supports several profitable chains.
Department stores cannot copy the opportunistic, no-advertised-price, lean store model without undercutting their own full-price business, which has helped TJX gain share as department stores shrank.

Its 1,400+ buyer organisation, 'open to buy' late buying, and flexible store and distribution system for fast-turning, ever-changing assortments have been refined since T.J. Maxx opened in 1977 and are hard to replicate.
Long vendor relationships and a deep bench of home-grown merchants matter, but no asset is exclusive.

customers.evidence: Consolidated comparable sales rose 4% in FY2025 and 5% in FY2026, then 6% in Q1 FY27 and 4% in Q2 FY27, driven mainly by customer transactions, showing frequent repeat 'treasure-hunt' visits; TJX ranked #2 among specialty retailers in Fortune's Most Admired Companies list.

talent.evidence: TJX employs about 377,000 associates and is known for training and promoting its own merchants (CEO Ernie Herrman joined as a buyer-track merchant in 1989), but most roles are hourly store jobs and it does not usually appear near the top of best-employer rankings.

product.evidence: For off-price retail it is the reference model: the widest range of brand-name apparel and home goods at 20-60% below full-price retailers' regular prices, which few rivals match outside the US and across both apparel and home.

competitors.name: Ross Stores (Ross Dress for Less, dd's DISCOUNTS)
competitors.note: Direct US off-price apparel and home rival with 2,267 stores; competes with Marmaxx and HomeGoods for both shoppers and vendor closeouts.

competitors.name: Burlington Stores
competitors.note: US off-price apparel, coats and home with 1,212 stores, competes directly with T.J. Maxx and Marshalls.

competitors.name: Nordstrom (Nordstrom Rack)
competitors.note: Nordstrom Rack off-price stores compete for upscale brand-name apparel and shoes; Nordstrom was taken private in 2025.

competitors.name: Walmart
competitors.note: Low-price apparel and home goods for the same value-seeking shoppers.

competitors.name: Target
competitors.note: Apparel and home decor with own brands at mid prices; overlaps with HomeGoods and Marmaxx.

competitors.name: Amazon.com
competitors.note: Online apparel, home goods and discounted branded products; a threat to store traffic.

competitors.name: Costco Wholesale
competitors.note: Treasure-hunt branded apparel and home items in warehouse clubs.

competitors.name: Kohl's
competitors.note: Moderate-priced department store apparel and home with heavy promotions.

competitors.name: Macy's
competitors.note: Department stores and Backstage off-price shops selling the same brands.

competitors.name: Ollie's Bargain Outlet
competitors.note: Closeout home goods and general merchandise.

competitors.name: Five Below
competitors.note: Low-price trend items and home decor for young shoppers.

competitors.name: Primark (Associated British Foods)
competitors.note: Low-price fashion competing with TK Maxx in the UK and Europe and expanding in the US.

competitors.name: PDD Holdings (Temu)
competitors.note: Ultra-cheap online apparel and home items.

competitors.name: Shein
competitors.note: Ultra-cheap online fast fashion aimed at value shoppers.

marketShare.market: US-listed off-price retailers (share of combined revenue of TJX, Ross Stores and Burlington; fiscal years ended Jan 2026 vs Jan 2023)

threats: A slowdown at Marmaxx, its largest division: Q2 FY27 Marmaxx comp sales rose only 1% and fell short of plan, while other divisions grew 6-7%.
Tariffs and trade policy raising merchandise costs; the size and timing of further IEEPA tariff refunds are uncertain, per the company.
A tighter supply of branded excess inventory if brands and department stores manage stock more precisely or run their own outlet channels.
Online ultra-cheap rivals (Temu, Shein, Amazon) taking value shoppers' spending.
Rising wage and freight costs squeezing a model built on low prices and about 377,000 mostly hourly associates.
Execution risk in international expansion (Spain, joint ventures in Mexico and the Middle East) where TJX International margins are lower (7.0% segment margin in FY2026).

ceo.name: Ernie Herrman
ceo.background: Career TJX merchant: joined in 1989 and rose through merchandising roles at Marmaxx, President of TJX since 2011, CEO since January 2016

c1.evidence: TJX leads off-price retail, but that is a mature industry growing at mid-single digits (FY2026 sales +7%), not a fast-growing emerging one.

c2.evidence: Shoppers choose it for brand-name goods at prices well below full-price retailers and a constantly changing 'treasure hunt' assortment, made possible by 1,400+ buyers and about 21,000 vendors, a scale advantage built since 1977 that rivals have not matched.

c3.evidence: T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods are household names and TJX is the default leader in off-price, but the parent name 'TJX' is less known and the business is not a category-defining brand like Amazon or Netflix.

c4.evidence: Its stated mission, 'to deliver great value to our customers every day', is clear and consistently repeated, but it is a commercial value promise rather than a world-changing purpose.

c6.evidence: “bargains, treasure hunt, brand names for less”: the public impression of T.J. Maxx, Marshalls and HomeGoods is mostly positive, though some associate the stores with messy racks and inconsistent selection.

c7.evidence: Its apparel and home markets are large and value-seeking shoppers are a lasting trend, but these markets grow only modestly; TJX's growth comes from share gains and store expansion toward a 7,500-store long-term target.

c8.evidence: It is entering Spain (from March 2026) and has joint ventures in Mexico and the Middle East, with a 7,500-store global target versus 5,285 stores in August 2026, but it stays within off-price retail.

m1.evidence: Ernie Herrman has a clear, consistent plan (more stores, new countries, steady comp growth) but is an operator focused on executing a proven model rather than a visionary reshaping the industry.

m2.evidence: Not a founder, but a 37-year TJX career merchant (joined 1989) who manages for the long term and preserves the company's culture.

m4.evidence: TJX paid a discretionary bonus to associates outside bonus plans from part of its FY2026 interchange settlement gain ($82 million), but there is little specific public evidence about Herrman's personal servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Herrman keeps a strong merchant-driven, frugal culture, but it is focused on buying and execution rather than inventing new products or technologies.

m6.evidence: He is deeply hands-on with merchandise as a career buyer and merchant, but has no engineering or technology background.

m7.evidence: No controversies are known and TJX runs community programmes for families and children, but there is no clear public evidence of a mission bigger than profit tied to Herrman personally.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Ernie Herrman at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Herrman keeps a low public profile and is not known for a distinctive public personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2016, sales have grown to $60.4 billion in FY2026 and pretax margin reached 12.1% in FY2026 from 9.1% in FY2022, with results 'well above plan' in Q4 FY26, Q1 FY27 and Q2 FY27.

m10.evidence: TJX's no-frills stores, minimal advertising and lean, opportunistic buying make frugality central to its model and culture.

c10.evidence: It saves millions of families in nine countries money on clothes and home goods, but it does not transform lives the way Google or Intuitive Surgical do.

p2.evidence: Running 5,000+ stores with fast-changing, opportunistically bought inventory is operationally hard to do well, but it is not a breakthrough technology or vital to the world.

f1.evidence: Net sales rose every year from FY2022 to FY2026: $48.55bn, $49.94bn, $54.22bn, $56.36bn, $60.37bn (after the pandemic year FY2021 at $32.14bn).

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 28.5% in FY2022 to 31.0% in FY2026 and operating margin from about 9.8% to 11.9% (calculated from 10-K figures).

f3.evidence: On August 1, 2026 TJX held $6,004 million cash against $2,871 million of debt, with $10,651 million shareholders' equity and $6,874 million FY2026 operating cash flow.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from about $4.76bn in FY2022 to $7.18bn in FY2026, and operating cash flow rose from $6,057 million in FY2024 to $6,874 million in FY2026.

v1.evidence: It is the largest and broadest off-price chain, with more brands and home goods than Ross or Burlington, but shoppers often see the three as similar and pick by location.

v2.evidence: TJX ranked #2 among specialty retailers in Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies, but it is not a regular at the top of best-employer rankings for its mostly hourly store workforce.

c5.evidence: Millions of bargain-hunting families and thousands of brand vendors that depend on it to clear excess stock would miss it, though Ross, Burlington and online rivals would fill much of the gap.
